CONTEXT. The previous page ('Litt. G') begins 'Neue Rechnung über den Cometen von 1772, wodurch demselben die für den 2 Cometen von 1805 gefundene elliptische Bahn angepaßt wird.' Gauss takes the elliptic elements found for the second comet of 1805 and tries to fit them to two observations of the comet of 1772. These two comets are now known to be apparitions of 3D/Biela. He keeps the elements fixed and varies only the perihelion time T (in days of February 1772). The fixed quantities are:
- log e = 9.8305400, so e = 0.67677;
- log(e·206265'') = 5.1449651;
- log sin(φ/2) = 9.5602436, where φ = arcsin e (φ/2 = 21°17.8');
- log of the mean daily motion in arcseconds = 2.8741241 (μ = 748.4''/day, period about 4.74 yr);
- log a = 0.4505887 (a = 2.822).

The previous page also prepared:
- two 'constants' with sin u = Const1/(r/a) and sin u' = Const2/(r'/a), where log Const1 = 9.5469096 and log Const2 = 9.5498659 (each already divided by a). Here u is an angle in the Sun–Earth–comet triangle fixed by the observed geocentric direction.
- a spherical formula for the heliocentric angle ('dist') between the two comet positions:
  sin(dist/2) = sqrt( cos²(A/2)·sin²((u'−u)/2 + 5°27'22.77'') + sin²(A/2)·sin²((u'+u)/2 + 2°58'42.84'') ),
  with log sin(A/2) = 8.5527368 and log cos(A/2) = 9.9997230.

For each trial T the 'Error' is dist − (v' − v), in arcseconds, where v and v' are the true anomalies from the orbit. Observation times are t1 = 55.37830 and t2 = 63.39858.

RESULTS CARRIED OVER FROM THE PREVIOUS PAGE.
- Hypothesis I: T = 11.22701, Error = −2356.14''.
- Hypothesis II: T = 12.22148. On that page this was first carried as −2732.95, and a secant step on that value gave T = 5.00873.

A. HYPOTHESIS III (T = 5.00873; 'Neue Hypothese').
- Times since perihelion: t − T = 50.36957 and 58.38985 (logs 1.7021683, 1.7663374).
- Mean anomalies: M = μ(t − T), log M = log(t − T) + 2.8741241, giving M1 = 37695.75'' = 10°28'15.75'' and M2 = 43697.990'' = 12°8'17.990''.
- Kepler's equation E − e''·sin E = M, solved by trial:
  - E1 = 29°40'9.472'', with e''·sin E1 = 19°11'53.722'';
  - E2 = 33°36'12.887'', with 21°27'54.897''.
  - Both subtractions check exactly against M1 and M2.
- Each orbit block has two columns.
  - Column 2: log e, log cos E, e·cos E (= 0.588181), log(1 − e cos E) = log(r/a) (= 9.6147102), then log(sin E·a/r) (= 0.0798890), then log sin v = log cos φ + log(sin E·a/r) (= 9.9467979).
  - Column 1: log e'', log sin E, (1/2)log(r/a) (= 9.8073551, exactly half of 9.6147102), log(sin E·sqrt(a/r)) (= 9.8872441), log sin(φ/2), and their sum log sin((v − E)/2) (= 9.4474877).
  - The formula used is sin((v − E)/2) = sin(φ/2)·sin E·sqrt(a/r) (Theoria Motus form).
  - Table interpolation gives (v − E)/2 = 16°16'20'' + (175/721)·10'' = 16°16'22.427''.
- Results: v1 = E1 + (v − E) = 29°40'9.472'' + 32°32'44.854'' = 62°12'54.33''. Likewise v2 = 33°36'12.887'' + 35°26'48.055'' = 69°3'0.942''.
- Orbit value: v' − v = 6°50'6.61'' ('III. 6°50'6''61').
- Geometry from the observations:
  - sin u = Const/(r/a): log sin u1 = 9.5469096 − 9.6147102, so u1 = 58°48'37.89''; u2 = 54°24'24.63''.
  - (u + u')/2 = 56°36'31.26''; adding 2°58'42.84'' gives 59°35'14.10''.
  - 5°27'22.77'' − 2°12'6.63'' = 3°15'16.14''.
  - Log products: 8.4884461 and 8.7538489.
  - The sum of squares is formed through an auxiliary angle (9.9439365), giving log sin(dist/2) = 8.8099124.
  - dist/2 = 3°42'4.15'', so dist = 7°24'8.31''.
- Error III = 7°24'8.31'' − 6°50'6.61'' = +34'1.70'' = +2041.70''.

B. ERROR LIST AND INVERSE QUADRATIC INTERPOLATION.
- Error list: I −2356.14 (T 11.22701); II −3124.13 (T 12.22148); III +2041.70 (T 5.00873). Value II is now the correct one.
- Gauss interpolates T as a quadratic (Lagrange) function of the error and evaluates it at error 0:
  T = w1·T1 − w2·T2 + w3·T3, with
  - w1 = 3124.13·2041.70/(767.99·4397.84),
  - w2 = 2356.14·2041.70/(767.99·5165.83),
  - w3 = 2356.14·3124.13/(4397.84·5165.83).
- Logs used:
  - 3.4947291 = log 3124.13, 3.3099919 = log 2041.70, 3.3722011 = log 2356.14;
  - 3.6432394 = log 4397.84, 2.8853556 = log 767.99, 3.7131401 = log 5165.83.
- He uses the rearranged form T = T1 − w2·(T2 − T1) − w3·(T1 − T3) (my identification, valid since w1 − w2 + w3 = 1):
  - log w2 = 0.0836973;
  - log w3 = 9.5105507;
  - log(T2 − T1) = 9.9975917, from 0.99447;
  - log(T1 − T3) = 0.7936703, from 6.21828.
- The two corrections are 1.20584 and 2.01475, summing to 3.22059. So T_IV = 11.22701 − 3.22059 = 8.00642 ('Zur neuen Hypothese').

C. HYPOTHESIS IV (T = 8.00642).
- t − T = 47.37188 and 55.39216, so M1 = 35452.325'' = 9°50'52.325'' and M2 = 41454.571'' = 11°30'54.571''.
- Anomalies:
  - E1 = 28°8'23.056'' (e·sin E = 18°17'30.731''), v1 − E1 = 31°18'42.897'', v1 = 59°27'5.953'';
  - E2 = 32°9'34.239'', v2 − E2 = 34°25'39.221'', v2 = 66°35'13.46''.
- Orbit value: v' − v = 7°8'7.51''.
- Geometry: u1 = 60°55'34.957'', u2 = 56°10'55.815'', giving 61°31'58.23'' and 3°5'3.20''. Then dist/2 = 3°34'10.51'', so dist = 7°8'21.02''.
- Error IV = +13.51''.

D. NEWTON-TYPE STEP.
- Secant slopes computed with logs:
  - (III,IV): 2028.19/2.99769 = 676.58, at mid-time 6.5076;
  - (I,III): 4397.84/6.21828 = 707.25, at 8.1179;
  - (IV,I): 2369.65/3.22059 = 735.78, at 9.6167.
- From these he interpolates a slope of 705.21''/day at T_IV.
  - The derivative of the parabola through III, IV, I at IV is s(III,IV) + s(IV,I) − s(III,I) = 705.11. That is essentially the same.
- Correction: 13.51/705.21 = 0.01916, so T_V = 8.02558 ('Zur Vten Hypothese').

E. HYPOTHESIS V (T = 8.02558).
- M1 = 35437.983'' = 9°50'37.983''; M2 = 41440.229'' = 11°30'40.229''.
- Anomalies:
  - E1 = 28°7'47.457'' (e·sin E = 18°17'9.474''), v1 = 59°26'0.924'';
  - E2 = 32°9'0.635'', v2 = 66°34'15.547''.
- Orbit value: v' − v = 7°8'14.62''.
- Geometry: u1 = 60°56'25.667'', u2 = 56°11'38.143'', giving 61°32'44.74'' and 3°4'59.01''. Then dist/2 = 3°34'7.29'', so dist = 7°8'14.59''.
- Error V = −0.03''. The fit has converged: with a and e of comet 1805 II, the 1772 observations are satisfied for T = Feb 8.02558.

F. BOTTOM OF PAGE: SPHERICAL TRIANGLES FOR THE NEXT PAGE.
- He solves the spherical triangles needed for the node and inclination on the next page, apparently with Napier-type analogies. Inputs:
  - log sin 61°32'44.74'' = 9.9440867;
  - log cos 61°32'44.74'' = 9.6780234;
  - log sin 3°4'59.01'' = 8.7306495;
  - log cos 3°4'59.01'' = 9.9993710;
  - log sin(A/2), log cos(A/2).
- 8.7306495 + 9.6780234 = 8.4086729; 9.9440867 + 9.9993710 = 9.9434577. Dividing gives tan x, x = 1°40'18.90''.
- A second pair gives 8.2307602 and 9.9990940.
- Resulting angles 89°1'24.00'' and 59°42'46.37'', combined as:
  - 89°1'24.00'' − 59°42'46.37'' = 29°18'37.63'';
  - 180° − 89°1'24.00'' − 59°42'46.37'' = 31°15'49.63''.
- These are the angles C' and C used on the next page. There, together with B = 30°44'8.06'' and B' = 31°12'1.98'', they give inclination 17°39', node 263°24' and ω.
- The exact formula for the 89°1'24'' / 59°42'46.37'' pair is not fully legible to me.
errors: Value II (T = 12.22148) was evidently carried on the previous page as −2732.95''; the correct value is −3124.13'' (7°34'42.39'' − 6°42'38.26''). The secant step there therefore produced the poor trial T = 5.00873. This page silently uses −3124.13 and repairs the damage by quadratic inverse interpolation, so the final result is unaffected.
The slope 705.21''/day differs slightly from the derivative of the interpolating parabola (705.11). The effect on the correction is negligible (0.019157 vs 0.019160 days; both round to 0.01916).
Small inconsistencies in interpolation fractions: for block IV, (v−E)/2 = 15°39'20'' + 108.5/751·10'' doubles to 31°18'42.89'' rather than the written 42.897''. This is at the 0.01'' level.

All Kepler-equation checks (E − e''·sin E = M), the differences v' − v, the dist values, the errors (+2041.70, +13.51, −0.03) and the Lagrange weights (w1 − w2 + w3 ≈ 1.0002) verify to the precision of 7-place logarithms.

results.what: Fitting the elliptic elements of comet 1805 II (Biela) to two 1772 observations by varying only the perihelion time; residual drops from thousands of arcseconds to 0.03''
results.modern_name: orbit linkage / identification of a periodic comet across apparitions (3D/Biela 1772–1805)
results.usually_credited_to: Identity of 1772, 1805 and 1826 comets established by Clausen and Gambart (1826) after Biela's rediscovery; resemblance of 1772 and 1805 noted earlier by Olbers/Gauss circle

results.what: sin((v−E)/2) = sin(φ/2)·sin E·sqrt(a/r), with e = sin φ, to get the true anomaly
results.modern_name: true anomaly from eccentric anomaly (Gaussian half-angle form)

results.what: Kepler's equation E − e sin E = M solved by trial with logarithms
Zero of the residual found by Lagrange interpolation of T as a quadratic in the error
results.modern_name: inverse quadratic interpolation (as in Brent/Muller-type root finding)
results.usually_credited_to: Lagrange interpolation (1795); inverse interpolation standard in 18th-c. astronomy

results.what: Final correction using a slope interpolated from three secant slopes (≈ derivative of the parabola at the latest point)
Spherical trigonometry (sum-of-squares formula for the heliocentric angle; Napier analogies) to prepare node and inclination

deep.surprise_reason: The techniques are routine Gaussian orbit computation. The content of interest is historical: a detailed 1805/06 computation showing that the 1772 comet can be represented with the elliptic orbit of comet 1805 II (Biela) to within a fraction of an arcsecond. The 1772/1805 resemblance was discussed in the Gauss–Olbers circle, and identity was formally established in 1826. So this is a notable but not revolutionary archival detail.
